facts.raw_span: an 8-month history of a growing, painful tumor on her right buttock
denied experiencing fevers, chills, sweats, weight loss, or malaise
chronic kidney disease
genital herpes simplex virus (HSV)
no history of genital warts, HIV, or inflammatory bowel disease
a 5 × 7-cm verrucous, exophytic tumor with scant yellow drainage on the right medial buttock extending to the perianal skin
Superficial bacterial cultures were obtained from the lesion and grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
Microbial cultures were negative for deep fungal infection and acid-fast bacteria
positive for HSV type 2
Hematoxylin-eosin stain showing hyperplastic epidermis with ulceration, necrosis, and dense inflammatory infiltrate
Hematoxylin-eosin stain showing plasma cells and focal multinucleated keratinocytes with gray-blue cytoplasm
Positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 within epithelial cells, including multinucleated keratinocytes

concepts.why: The patient presents with a growing, painful tumor on her right buttock, which is described as a 5 × 7-cm verrucous, exophytic tumor with scant yellow drainage, and histology shows hyperplastic epidermis with ulceration, necrosis, and dense inflammatory infiltrate.
The patient has a history of genital herpes simplex virus and the lesion is positive for HSV type 2, with positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 within epithelial cells.
Superficial bacterial cultures from the lesion grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
The patient has a notable medical history of chronic kidney disease.

concepts.preferred_label: Verrucous carcinoma with herpes simplex virus infection
concepts.why: The presence of multinucleated keratinocytes with gray-blue cytoplasm and positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 within epithelial cells explains the uncovered fact of Hematoxylin-eosin stain showing plasma cells and focal multinucleated keratinocytes with gray-blue cytoplasm.

rationales.F01: The presence of a growing, painful tumor is more typical of verrucous carcinoma and verrucous carcinoma with herpes simplex virus infection.
rationales.F03: Chronic kidney disease is a known comorbidity, but it does not directly relate to the other concepts.
rationales.F04: The history of genital herpes simplex virus infection increases the likelihood of herpes simplex virus infection.
rationales.F06: The description of the tumor is highly suggestive of verrucous carcinoma and verrucous carcinoma with herpes simplex virus infection.
rationales.F07: The presence of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection is a significant finding for this concept.
rationales.F09: The positive culture for HSV type 2 supports the diagnosis of herpes simplex virus infection and verrucous carcinoma with herpes simplex virus infection.
rationales.F10: The histological findings of hyperplastic epidermis with ulceration, necrosis, and dense inflammatory infiltrate are consistent with verrucous carcinoma and verrucous carcinoma with herpes simplex virus infection.
rationales.F11: The presence of plasma cells and focal multinucleated keratinocytes with gray-blue cytoplasm is consistent with verrucous carcinoma and verrucous carcinoma with herpes simplex virus infection.
rationales.F12: The positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 within epithelial cells, including multinucleated keratinocytes, strongly supports the diagnosis of herpes simplex virus infection and verrucous carcinoma with herpes simplex virus infection.
